Why so many Indian houses have steel rods sticking out of the roof

Those rods are the tops of the columns, left there on purpose. Many Indian homes are built floor by floor, as money comes in. Leave the rods out and the next floor's columns can lock into the old ones. Cut them off, and later someone has to drill into the columns and glue new bars in.

The catch: bare steel rusts, and rust can take up to six times the volume of the steel it eats. Rain running down the rods into the column can crack the concrete from the inside.

Rods on your roof: future floor, or future crack? Tell us below.

Send this to the family that has been "adding a floor next year" for 10 years.

Sources: AMPP Materials Performance (rust volume), US FHWA corrosion research, Hilti post-installed rebar guidance, The Tribune (column cover and rust), Nepali Times and Sketchplanations (building in stages).
Photos: Asad Younis Tanoli, Deep Doshi, Thakur Jaideep Singh, miguel garcia jimenez, Abhinav Anand, Zoshua Colah, Rob Dean, Muhammad Sharifuz / Unsplash. Diagrams are illustrations, not to scale.
Educational content, not structural advice.

instagram_media.caption:
How Burj Khalifa stands on sand

The tallest building on Earth has no solid bedrock under it. Below Dubai is loose sand, then about 70 m of weak sandstone, with salty groundwater just 2.5 m down.

The fix: 192 concrete piles, each 1.5 m wide and about 50 m deep, holding mostly by friction. On top sits a 3.7 m thick raft. The foundations alone used about 110,000 tonnes of concrete, and an electric cathodic protection system guards the steel from the salt.

So is it standing on sand, or gripping it?

Send this to the friend who has been to Dubai.

Sources: Arabian Business (How Burj was built), Bunce and Poulos foundation design via GeoPrac, TheConstructor case study.
Photos: Pavlo Antonio, Timo Volz, Ahmed Aldaie / Unsplash. Cutaways are AI visualisation.
Educational content, not advice.

instagram_media.caption:
Stamp duty in Delhi, Gurugram and Noida: same ₹1 crore flat, very different bill.

Whose name is on the sale deed changes what you pay to register it.
Delhi: 6% for men, 4% for women, 5% joint, plus 1% registration.
Gurugram (Haryana urban): 7% men, 5% women, 6% joint, registration capped at ₹50,000.
Noida (UP): 7%, with a 1% rebate for women on property up to ₹1 crore, plus 1% registration.

Stamp duty is charged on the deal value or the circle rate, whichever is higher. Rates change, so check the state portal before you register. The person named becomes the legal owner.

Send this to whoever is deciding whose name goes on the flat.

Sources: Delhi and UP rates via NoBroker (Nov 2026) and HomeFirst (Jun 2026); Haryana via ClearTax; UP cabinet decision, News On AIR (23 Jul 2025).
Photo: Ankur Khandelwal / Unsplash. Still lifes are AI visualisation.
Educational content, not legal or tax advice.
